catalog_citation: Honda, Isao. 2002. Seke phonology: a comparative study of three Seke dialects. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 25(1): 191-210. DOI 10.32655/ltba.25.1.08.
catalog_locator: Sec. 2 'Tone', pp. 193-194 (PDF pp. 3-4); LTBA 25(1), sealang.net archive scan (image-only; read from the page images).
catalog_quote: Like all the other Tamangic languages except Chantyal (cf. Noonan et al. 1998:2, Noonan to appear a), all three dialects of Seke have a four-tone system. The basic character of the Seke tone system is not different from those of other Tamangic dialects. ... The Tangbe tone system is described in Honda (to appear), which follows Mazaudon's (1973a, 1973b, 1978) analysis of the Risiangku dialect of Eastern Tamang and other Tamangic dialects. According to Mazaudon's analysis, the domain of the Tamangic tone is not the syllable but the phonological word, and there are four word-tone classes. She calls them tones 1, 2, 3 and 4, respectively. The four tones can be distinguished by their pitch contours. ... [p. 194:] Except in Taglung, Ngawal and Marpha, there is a major contrast between the two high tones (tone 1 and tone 2) and the two low tones (tone 3 and tone 4). Under the high tones, unaspirated stops and affricates that occur in word-initial position are usually realized as voiceless. Under the low tones, on the other hand, they are usually realized as voiced, and the vowel occurring in the word-initial syllable is pronounced with breathy voice. Because of those features, the high-low distinction is easy to hear. This is also the case for the three Seke dialects. ... The phonetic values of the four tones have not been measured in any dialects of Seke, but those in Tangbe can be inferred from the data provided by Mazaudon (1996)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Seke (Tangbe, Tetang, Chuksang) is described as a four-way word-tone language of the Tamangic type: the tone's domain is the phonological word, not the syllable; two high tones (Tangbe 54, 43) vs two low tones (21, 11) with breathy voice on the word-initial syllable under low tone. The article contains no statement about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; author notes the tone-1/2 and tone-3/4 distinctions are hard to elicit (few minimal pairs) and that Tangbe pitch values are inferred, not measured.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone domain = phonological word (word-tone); nothing on phrase-level prominence or citation-form stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Honda 2002 covers three Seke dialects (Tangbe, Tetang, Chuksang; Chaile and Gyakar grouped with Chuksang); the tone pitch values quoted are for Tangbe. Glottolog seke1240 lists no sub-dialect codes. Not to be confused with Seke of Vanuatu (seke1241) or Gabonese Seki.
